newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire gears up for more fighting as talks planned.
newsitem.headline: Zaire gears up for more fighting as talks planned.

text.p: Zaire is preparing to defend a key town on the path of advancing rebels and will resume aerial bombing, defence ministry officials said on Monday.
South Africa announced plans for summit talks to contain Zaire's expanding four-month rebel war but diplomats in Kinshasa said fighting looked likely to escalate before then.

A senior defence official denied foreign radio reports that rebels, who took the mining town of Kalima on Saturday, were heading for Kindu, the Maniema Province capital and one of Zaire's principal military bases in the region.
"We have taken necessary steps to defend Kindu and we will be attacking Kalima and Kalemie by plane shortly," the official said. The inland port of Kalemie fell to rebels this month.
The spokesman for rebel leader Laurent Kabila said in eastern Zaire that Kindu, 80 km (50 miles) southwest of Kalima, was the next target.
"We have been holding back on making military advances while the negotiations have been initiated," said Raphael Ghenda.
Zaire planes last week bombed the rebel-held towns of Bukavu, Shabunda and Walekali, killing at least 19 people and prompting a threat of revenge from rebel chief Laurent Kabila.
The Zairean official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters reports of rebel advances were speculation started by Kabila's threat of a generalised offensive.
There appeared to be little optimism among diplomats in Kinshasa that a negotiated settlement was in sight.
"Kabila may be prepared to attend talks at least to show that he is willing, but it is unlikely he will abandon the military effort while he is accumulating victories," one said.
South African President Nelson Mandela said on Monday he and other African leaders would meet Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko on March 19 in a new bid to end civil war in Zaire.
Mandela told reporters negotiators would deal separately with Kabila, who shunned a Cape Town peace meeting on Zaire at the weekend.
"Our first step is to see President Mobutu. There are initiatives to deal with Mr Kabila, but the first step is not to bring the two of them together," Mandela said.
The spokesman for Kabila said in eastern Zaire that the rebels "viewed positively" any peace initiative.

"We don't have all the information about this most recent development out of South Africa but we view positively any measures taken by the international community for negotiations to resolve the Zaire conflict," said Ghenda.
Mandela said he and leaders of countries around Zaire, including Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia and Congo, would meet Mobutu in Nairobi or in Gbadolite, Zaire, on March 19.
Kinshasa has denied knowledge of the talks in South Africa and Mobutu was again quoted on Monday as ruling out negotiations with rebels bent on ending his 31-year rule.

"The Zairean government and President Mobutu seek the withdrawal, pure and simple, of all foreign troops from Zairean territory," Mobutu's son and spokesman Mobutu Nzanga told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Since last Friday Mobutu has been at his villa on the French Riviera where he has spent much of the time since prostate cancer surgery last August.

Ethnic Tutsis took up arms in October after local authorities tried to force them to Rwanda, their ancestral home. Zaire says they are backed by soldiers from Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda. All deny the charge.

Rebels now hold a 1,000-km (600 miles) strip stretching from the war's starting point on the Rwanda border to Zaire's important southern copper-producing province of Shaba. Defence officials said the front in Shaba had stabilised around the town of Fatuma, about 100 km (60 miles) south of Kalemie.

Western intelligence sources said Zaire was struggling to restore order to at least a part of its mercenary-backed army based in Kisangani. But they said these efforts had yet to show any sign of success on the ground.
